meta.program: The Hype Filter · Thrive Thursday · Anchor's Edge · Vanderbilt
meta.audience: All Vanderbilt staff in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm; no management experience assumed. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; April is the Spot AI-Exposed Work month, and this session closes the week.
meta.roomSetup: Virtual, instructor led: camera on, deck link in chat, breakouts of 2 available. Learners follow on their own screens via the welcome-slide link or QR. Nothing typed into the deck is saved or sent.
meta.postSession: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did the filter run on your claim? What was the verdict, and which test decided it? Which claim is next?' Count of completed filter runs is the Level 3 metric for the month.

full.description: The full 45-minute virtual session: every interaction runs live, breakouts run in pairs, and the capstone gets read-alouds. The per-section minutes on each slide sum to 45 including transitions.

core.description: The 30-minute slot: agenda and core-idea slides pass in stride, breakouts become solo passes with chat share-outs, debriefs shrink to one voice. Never cut the section interactions or the capstone.

meta.framework: ATD facilitator-guide structure: per module SAY / DO / ASK (with anticipated responses) / DEBRIEF / TRANSITION, plus preparation checklists, materials, contingencies, and a tough-questions bank.
materials: Meeting platform with screen share and breakout rooms; deck link ready to paste in chat
Facilitator machine with the facilitator edition open; notifications off
Learners on their own devices with the learner link
Chat open for share-outs; the capstone copy button pastes there cleanly

weekBefore: Run the learner edition start to finish and do every interaction honestly; you will demo at least one live.
Read this month's theme page on the Anchor's Edge dashboard so the goal tie-in is fluent.
Send the invite with the learner link and one line on what to bring.
dayBefore: Test screen share with the facilitator edition; confirm the notes rail is readable.
Open the learner link on a second device; the QR must land there.
Run the section interactions once so you can drive them without reading.
thirtyMinBefore: Welcome slide up as people join; link pasted in chat.
Close every other tab; silence the machine.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: The room turns the session into complaints about a specific vendor or product
contingencies.then: Steer back to the pattern: no verdicts on named products here. The filter is the takeaway, and it outlives any one tool. Keep the examples generic.

contingencies.if: Someone argues the beneficiary test makes them distrust colleagues
contingencies.then: Reframe warmly: the test is about incentives, never character. A colleague can be sincere and wrong at the same time; the evidence test catches that, and the beneficiary test simply asks who is selling.

toughQuestions.q: Isn't this just teaching us to be cynical about AI?
toughQuestions.a: The filter fails hype and passes value, and it runs in both directions: dismissing a genuinely useful tool is exactly as unfiltered as buying the demo. The colleague claim in the trainer passes cleanly. Skepticism that names its own mind-changer is called judgment.

toughQuestions.q: What if leadership has already decided to adopt a tool the filter would fail?
toughQuestions.a: The filter still helps: it tells you what evidence to gather during rollout. Name the mind-changer, run your own tasks through the tool, and report what you find. Honest evidence from real use is valuable to leadership in both directions, and Goal 3 explicitly asks for it.

toughQuestions.q: Where does the traffic light fit into testing new tools?
toughQuestions.a: Every test rides the light. A trial uses public or generic content freely; internal content only inside approved VU tools; and private information about people never goes into a test, no matter how promising the tool. An unapproved tool gets tested with green content only, if at all.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Thursday, 45 minutes on sorting AI hype from real value. Bring one claim you have heard about AI this month, from any source; you will run it through a three-question filter. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: What was the verdict? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did the filter run on the claim from your card? 2) What was the verdict, and which test decided it? 3) Which claim gets filtered next?

sections.title: Welcome / QR
sections.purpose: Get everyone into the deck on their own screen and set the tone: 45 minutes, live, hands on.
sections.say: Welcome to Thrive Thursday. Scan the code or click the link in chat so this session runs on your screen too. Forty-five minutes, one focus: Softskill · Critical thinking: sorting hype from value.
facilitate: Slide up as people join; link pasted in chat every few minutes.
State the norm once: type into your own screen, nothing you enter is saved or sent.
sections.watchFor: People lurking without the deck open. The interactions only land if the deck is on their screen.
sections.transition: Before the topic, thirty seconds on why Vanderbilt is asking for this hour.

sections.title: Why we're here
sections.purpose: Anchor the session in the Chancellor's charge and name the goal this month serves, inside one minute.
sections.say: One sentence from the Chancellor sits over everything we do: Vanderbilt will define the great university of the 21st Century and be it. Staff who test claims before believing them keep Radical Collaboration honest, with shared decisions built on evidence rather than volume. This month serves Goal 3, AI-Enabled Workforce Readiness.
facilitate: Read the mission line slowly, once; name the goal, once.
No discussion here; the whole slide is under a minute.
sections.transition: Here is what you will be able to do in 45 minutes.

sections.title: Objectives
sections.purpose: Set the contract for the session in about a minute; this slide is also the roadmap.
sections.say: By the end of this session you will be able to: run any claim through three tests: the evidence, the beneficiary, and the mind-changer; spot the hype tells: big numbers, no baseline, urgency, and a seller in the byline; apply the filter to one real tool-adoption decision this week. We take them in order, and each one has something to practice.
facilitate: Read the three objectives briskly; they double as the agenda.
Point at the goal chip once, then move.

sections.title: The three tests
sections.purpose: Install the filter: evidence, beneficiary, mind-changer, one minute per claim.
sections.say: This week your manager mapped exposure and Tuesday you sorted your own tasks. Today is the quality control for all of it, because every map and every sort rests on claims about what AI can do. Three questions, one minute: what is the evidence, who benefits from my believing this, and what would change my mind?
facilitate: Read the three tests slowly, once each, then bring up the In the room card.
Run the discussion prompt: one half-believed claim and the test it wobbles on. Take two or three voices.
Run the breakout: one recent AI claim through all three tests.

ask.q: Which of the three tests do you skip most often?
expect: Some admit the beneficiary test feels cynical
A few say they rarely see the evidence at all
ask.respond: The mind-changer is the one that separates reasoning from believing, and it is the cheapest: one honest sentence before you decide.

sections.debrief: The filter is a habit, and habits need to be fast: three questions before a claim gets your belief, whichever direction it leans. Enthusiasm and dismissal both get filtered.
sections.watchFor: People aiming the filter only at claims they already dislike. The tests work on your favorite claims too, and that is where they earn the most.
sections.transition: The tests are simple. Hearing when to reach for them takes a tuned ear.
sections.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; ask for one recent claim in chat instead.

sections.title: The hype tells
sections.purpose: Tune learners' ears to the recurring patterns of hype and the sound of checkable value.
sections.say: Hype is lazy; it repeats itself. Giant numbers with no baseline. Urgency that evaporates when you check the calendar. Sellers quoted as judges of their own product. Value sounds different: a named task, a real number with a before and after, and an invitation to check. And when the claim is about what AI can do at all, there is an independent scoreboard: Stanford publishes the AI Index every year, measuring capability and adoption with nothing to sell. Let's tune your ear on three claims.
facilitate: Run Hype or value? live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After the colleague claim, pause: ask what makes it so much more credible than the vendor's.
Run the breakout: one pitches pure hype, one filters out loud, then swap.

ask.q: Why does the colleague's claim pass the beneficiary test so cleanly?
expect: They gain nothing from your belief
They offered the before and after
The task is specific and close to yours
ask.respond: Right. And notice that the offer to show the work is itself a tell: value invites checking, hype discourages it.

sections.debrief: Hype stacks its tells: big, vague, urgent, interested. Value is specific, checkable, and calm. The unclear middle deserves a cheap test before belief.
sections.watchFor: Cynics using the session to dismiss every AI claim. The filter passes real value too; the colleague claim exists so the room feels the difference.
sections.transition: A tuned ear is good. A decision method is better.
sections.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one voice on the debrief question.

sections.title: The live decision
sections.purpose: Turn the filter into a decision method: own-work evidence and a mind-changer named in advance.
sections.say: Here is where the filter stops being commentary and starts making decisions. When a tool claim reaches your team, the answer is rarely an instant yes or no. It is a small test on your own real work, with the bar named before the test runs: it wins if it saves an hour with no accuracy loss. Set the bar first and the result settles it, whichever way it lands.
facilitate: Run Design the deciding test; give the room two minutes for both choices.
Ask one volunteer to read a weak outcome aloud; let the room name the missing test.
Point at the pattern: own-work evidence, bar set in advance.

ask.q: Why does naming the mind-changer before the trial change the whole decision?
expect: It stops both sides claiming victory
It makes the trial evidence instead of theater
It protects the decision from the loudest voice
ask.respond: All three. A bar set in advance is the cheapest honesty mechanism a team can buy, and it works on far more than AI tools.

sections.debrief: The deciding test: one real recurring task, an approved VU tool, output checked against today's way, and the winning condition written down first.
sections.watchFor: People designing trials on vendor sample data. Redirect to their own recurring tasks; borrowed data proves nothing about their week.
sections.transition: Quick recap, then a real claim goes on your card.
sections.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.purpose: Land the one sentence the session exists to install.
sections.say: If you keep one sentence from today, this is it. Read it once, out loud: Run every AI claim through the three tests before you act on it or repeat it.
facilitate: Pause two beats after reading; the word animation carries it.
sections.coreNote: Core: pass through in stride; the sentence reads itself.

sections.title: Recap quiz
sections.purpose: Score the learning while it is fresh; wrong answers are teaching moments, not failures.
sections.say: Three questions, on your own screen. Answer honestly; the explanations are where the learning sticks.
facilitate: Give the room 90 seconds to run it individually.
Ask for a show of results in chat: how many got 3 of 3?
Read out the explanation for whichever question drew the most misses.
sections.watchFor: Rushing past the why lines. The explanations carry the teaching.
sections.transition: Now point it at your real week.

sections.title: Capstone commitment
sections.purpose: Convert the session into one named, dated action per person.
sections.say: Now pick your claim. Something actually circling your work: a tool pitch, a headline, a hallway certainty. Choose how you run the filter, pick the window, build the card, and copy it somewhere you will see it. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitate: Two quiet minutes; everyone builds their own card.
Invite two or three volunteers to read their card aloud or paste it in chat.
Remind: copy the card somewhere you will see it this week.
sections.watchFor: Vague entries. Nudge for a name-able situation and a real date.

sections.title: Closing
sections.purpose: End with the next step and where this thread continues.
sections.say: That closes the April week: your manager can map exposure, your week is sorted into tasks, and every claim now meets three questions before it meets your belief. If you want to keep pulling the thread, the LinkedIn Learning course AI for Leaders by Doug Rose is this month's companion, and the navigator-led exposure mapping workshop takes whole teams through Monday's map together. Next week the series turns to May's theme, Measured Leader Behavior, where the honest evidence habit you built today keeps right on working. See you Monday.
facilitate: Point at the next-step card; one sentence.
Name the rest of the week's rhythm: the other sessions echo this month's theme.
